snip.t: Female mite burrows into stratum corneum $\rightarrow$ Lays eggs $\rightarrow$ Larvae hatch and migrate $\rightarrow$ Sensitization to mite antigens $\rightarrow$ Intense pruritus.
Pruritus (itching): Due to uremic frost or electrolyte imbalances.
Uraemia: Pericarditis, encephalopathy, gastrointestinal bleeding, pruritus.
Skin – Pruritus, pallor, petechiae = uremic platelet dysfunction.

qs.q: A 53-year-old man with unresectable pancreatic head cancer presents with severe intractable jaundice and pruritus. An external drainage catheter is placed as an emergency measure. What defines the primary mechanism of this specific drainage type?
o: A. Draining bile entirely into an external bag via proximal side holes
B. Allowing bidirectional flow through side holes placed across the ampulla
C. Routing bile through a surgically created loop of jejunum to colon
D. Placing self-expanding metal stents across stricture for internal flow
qs.e: External drainage uses a catheter with side holes placed proximal to the obstruction, draining bile entirely into an external collection bag. Stents and internal-external paths allow drainage into the gastrointestinal tract.
qs.s: PTC and Percutaneous Biliary Drainage in Obstructive Jaundice: MCQs

qs.q: A 58-year-old man with long-standing end-stage renal disease presents with diffuse bone pain and generalized pruritus. Laboratory studies show hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated intact parathyroid hormone levels. What is the primary driving mechanism for the parathyroid findings?
o: Paraneoplastic production of parathyroid hormone
Autonomous hyperplasia from calcium receptor mutation
Compensatory response to renal failure
Parautocrine secretion by a single adenoma
qs.e: Chronic renal failure causes impaired calcitriol production and hyperphosphatemia, resulting in hypocalcemia that drives secondary parathyroid hyperplasia. A solitary parathyroid adenoma causes primary hyperparathyroidism, not the four-gland hyperplasia seen in renal failure.
qs.s: Year 3: Endocrine and Metabolic Pathology: MCQs

qs.q: A hospitalized patient receiving rapid intravenous vancomycin infusion develops sudden flushing, erythema, and pruritus over the upper torso and neck. What is the appropriate classification of this adverse event?
o: Severe drug-induced nephrotoxicity leading to acute tubular necrosis
Direct histamine release rather than a true IgE-mediated drug allergy
Type I immediate hypersensitivity reaction requiring immediate epinephrine
Irreversible cochlear ototoxicity mediated through reactive oxygen species
qs.e: Red Man Syndrome is caused by direct infusion-rate-dependent histamine release from mast cells, which is managed by slowing the infusion rather than treating it as an immunologic allergy. It is distinct from true anaphylaxis or vancomycin-induced nephrotoxicity.

qs.q: A 33-year-old woman develops localized flushing, pruritus, and urticaria 10 minutes after starting a red blood cell transfusion. What is the appropriate initial intervention?
o: Stop transfusion immediately and initiate cardiopulmonary resuscitation
Stop or slow transfusion and administer antihistamines
Stop transfusion and administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
Place patient upright and administer loop diuretics
qs.e: Flushing, itching, and urticaria indicate a mild allergic reaction, managed by slowing or stopping the infusion and giving antihistamines. Diuretics, antibiotics, and CPR are reserved for fluid overload, sepsis, and severe anaphylaxis, respectively.

qs.q: A patient presents with jaundice, dark urine, pale clay-coloured stools, and severe pruritus. Blood tests reveal elevated conjugated bilirubin. What is the primary cause of the pruritus in this patient?
o: Accumulation of unconjugated bilirubin
Elevated circulating bile salts
Excessive red blood cell haemolysis
Systemic inflammation from infection
qs.e: Pruritus in obstructive jaundice is caused by elevated bile salts in the circulation due to biliary obstruction. Pre-hepatic jaundice involves unconjugated bilirubin and does not typically cause pruritus or pale stools.
qs.s: Gastrointestinal System: Symptoms, Diseases, & VINDICATE Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with obstructive jaundice complains of generalized pruritus. What is the underlying biochemical cause of the itching in this condition?
o: Deposition of excessive stercobilinogen in peripheral tissues
Elevated circulation of bile salts
Systemic release of histamine secondary to hepatocyte necrosis
Accumulation of unconjugated bilirubin in the dermis
qs.e: Pruritus in obstructive jaundice is directly caused by elevated bile salts in the circulation. Unconjugated bilirubin does not cause this specific type of pruritus seen in biliary obstruction.
qs.s: Gastrointestinal System: Symptoms, Diseases, & VINDICATE Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A 24-year-old woman presents with a frothy greenish-yellow vaginal discharge and vulvar pruritus. A saline wet mount of the discharge examined under a light microscope reveals which characteristic finding confirming the diagnosis?
o: Gram-positive intracellular diplococci
Jerky, twitching motility of trophozoites
Cysts containing four distinct nuclei
Budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae
qs.e: Saline wet mounts characteristically show pear-shaped trophozoites exhibiting a jerky, twitching motility alongside leukocytes. Budding yeast points toward candidiasis rather than trichomoniasis.

qs.q: Which autoantibody is classically positive in Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC), a condition involving bile duct destruction and pruritus?
o: Antinuclear antibody marker
Tissue transglutaminase antibody
Anti-smooth muscle antibody
Anti-mitochondrial antibody
qs.e: Primary Biliary Cholangitis is characterized by bile duct destruction and is positive for anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA). Antinuclear and smooth muscle antibodies are typically seen in autoimmune hepatitis.
qs.s: Clinical Chemical Pathology Crash Course — Part 2: MCQs

es.q: A patient presents with pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools. Lab results show significantly elevated Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP) and Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), along with elevated conjugated bilirubin. a) What is the most likely hepatic injury pattern indicated by these findings? b) Explain
es.m: a) The most likely hepatic injury pattern is cholestasis. b) Pruritus occurs due to the systemic retention and deposition of bile salts in the skin. c) Two other clinical consequences include skin xanthomas (due to cholesterol deposits) and malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A patient presents with generalized pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools. Lab results show markedly elevated serum Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and GGT, along with elevated conjugated bilirubin. What is the most likely hepatic pathological process, and name two other specific clinical features associ
es.m: The most likely pathological process is cholestasis. Other clinical features include jaundice (due to elevated bilirubin) and skin xanthomas (due to cholesterol deposits). Malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) is also characteristic.
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A medical examiner receives liver function test (LFT) results for a deceased individual showing significantly elevated Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT), with normal ALT and AST levels. The individual's clinical history indicates pruritus and pale stools. What is the mo
es.m: The most likely pattern of liver pathology suggested by these findings is **cholestasis** (impaired bile flow) or biliary obstruction. **Correlation with Findings and Symptoms:** * **Elevated ALP and GGT (with normal ALT/AST):** This pattern is highly indicative of biliary excretory dysfunction, specifically cholestasis. ALP is a marker found in bile duct epithelial cells, and GGT is also elevated in biliary disease. * **Normal ALT and AST:** The absence of significant elevation in hepatocyte integrity markers (ALT, AST) indicates that widespread hepatocellular injury is not the primary issue. * **Pruritus:** This is a classic clinical feature of cholestasis, caused by the deposition of bile
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

es.q: A patient presents with jaundice, pruritus, and pale stools. What specific laboratory findings would you expect in their Liver Function Tests (LFTs) based on these clinical features, and which type of bilirubin would be predominantly elevated?
es.m: The clinical features (jaundice, pruritus, pale stools) strongly suggest cholestasis. Based on this, the expected LFT findings related to biliary excretory function would be: 1. Significantly elevated Alkaline phosphatase (ALP). 2. Elevated Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT). 3. Predominantly elevated conjugated bilirubin.
es.s: Liver Histology, Physiology and Pathology — Practice Questions

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Pruritus is an unpleasant skin sensation that provokes scratching. It can be a symptom of systemic disease, dermatologic disorder, or drug reaction, and its evaluation must be guided by history, exam, and targeted investigations, especially where resources are limited.

sections.p: Pruritus is the perception of itch leading to a desire to scratch. Diagnosis is clinical, based on patient description, distribution, and associated features.
b: Ask about onset, duration, pattern (continuous vs intermittent), aggravating/relieving factors.
Identify primary vs secondary lesions (scratch marks, excoriations).

sections.p: Severity is graded by impact on sleep, daily activities, and mental health. The Visual Analogue Scale (0‑10) or 5‑point Likert scale is practical.
b: Mild: ≤3/10, no sleep disturbance.
Moderate: 4‑6/10, occasional sleep loss.
Severe: ≥7/10, frequent sleep loss, anxiety or depression.

sections.p: In East African and similar low‑resource hospitals, common aetiologies are grouped by organ system and prevalence.
b: Dermatologic: scabies, atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, fungal infections.
Renal: chronic kidney disease (uremic pruritus).
Hepatobiliary: cholestasis from viral hepatitis, gallstone disease, primary biliary cholangitis.
Infectious: HIV‑related skin disease, malaria‑related urticaria, schistosomiasis dermatitis.
Hematologic: iron‑deficiency anaemia, polycythaemia vera, lymphoma.
Drug‑induced: antiretrovirals, antihypertensives, antibiotics.

sections.p: Itching may be localized (e.g., scabies in web spaces) or generalized (e.g., uremic). Look for secondary skin changes and systemic clues.
b: Localized papular rash with burrows → scabies.
Generalised excoriations, dry skin → renal or cholestatic.
Yellowish discoloration of sclera or skin → cholestasis.
Night‑time worsening, weight loss → HIV or malignancy.

t.b: Detect anaemia, eosinophilia, leukocytosis; eosinophilia suggests parasitic or allergic cause.
Assess renal function; eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m² supports uremic pruritus.

t.a: Liver function tests (ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin)
t.b: Identify cholestatic pattern (ALP ≫ ALT) indicating hepatobiliary cause.
Positive test directs evaluation toward HIV‑related dermatoses.
Finding mites or eggs confirms scabies; if microscopy unavailable, treat empirically based on clinical picture.
Elevated IgE supports atopic or parasitic aetiology.

sections.p: Uncontrolled scratching can lead to secondary infection, cellulitis, or sepsis, especially in immunocompromised patients.
b: Rapidly spreading erythema with warmth → cellulitis.
Fever, chills, or lymphangitis → systemic infection.
New onset severe pruritus with jaundice → possible cholestatic liver disease.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; then provide symptomatic relief while avoiding agents unavailable or unsafe in low‑resource settings.
b: Renal: optimise dialysis adequacy; consider low‑dose gabapentin if available.
Dermatologic: topical 1 % permethrin overnight for scabies; emollients for dry skin.
Antihistamines: non‑sedating (e.g., cetirizine) for allergic itch; sedating (e.g., diphenhydramine) at night to improve sleep.
Avoid: systemic steroids unless severe inflammatory dermatosis, due to infection risk.

sections.p: Re‑assess itch severity after 2‑3 weeks of therapy and monitor for complications.
b: Educate patients on skin hygiene, avoidance of known irritants, and proper use of emollients.
In endemic areas, periodic de‑worming and malaria prophylaxis reduce parasite‑related itch.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic pruritus or share similar descriptors.
b: Painful neuropathic burning (e.g., diabetic neuropathy) – distinguish by burning quality and lack of scratching.
Urticaria – transient wheals that resolve within 24 h, unlike persistent itch.

sections.p: Laboratory values may be normal early or altered by co‑existing disease.
b: Normal ALP does not exclude early cholestasis; repeat if clinical suspicion persists.
Eosinophil count may be normal in chronic scabies; rely on clinical signs.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe generalized pruritus with jaundice or hepatic encephalopathy signs

faq.q: Why does kidney failure cause itching?
faq.a: Uremic toxins and secondary hyperparathyroidism stimulate nerve endings and alter skin barrier, producing pruritus.
They provide limited relief; bile‑acid sequestrants target the pathophysiology more effectively.

faq.q: Is scabies contagious in the hospital?
faq.a: Yes; treat patient and close contacts, and wash bedding/clothing at 60 °C to stop transmission.

exam: What is the first investigation for a patient with new‑onset generalized pruritus and jaundice? — Check liver function tests; a cholestatic pattern (ALP ≫ ALT) points to hepatobiliary disease.
A dialysis patient complains of severe itch despite adequate dialysis. Which drug is most appropriate next? — Start cholestyramine to bind bile acids; gabapentin can be added if available.
How would you differentiate scabies from atopic dermatitis on exam? — Look for burrows in finger webs and wrists; atopic dermatitis shows flexural eczema without burrows.

A HIV‑positive patient has generalized pruritus and excoriations but normal eosinophils. What is your next step? — Perform skin scrapings for opportunistic infections and treat empirically for HIV‑related dermatoses while awaiting results.
Why should systemic steroids be avoided in a patient with pruritic papular eruption in a malaria‑endemic area? — Steroids suppress immunity and may worsen underlying infection.
What red‑flag sign would prompt immediate referral for a patient with pruritus? — Development of cellulitis with fever or signs of sepsis.
Explain why a normal ALP does not rule out early biliary obstruction. — Early obstruction may not yet raise ALP; imaging (ultrasound) is needed if clinical suspicion remains.
